lessons.title: How Fresher Interviews Work: Rounds and What to Expect
lessons.description: Understand the usual stages of a fresher hiring process, from application to offer, and what each round is really testing, in India, the UK, Canada and Africa.

content.text: Your first interview feels scary mostly because it is unknown. Nobody has told you what happens, how long it takes, or what the people on the other side are looking for. This lesson removes the mystery. When you can picture the whole process, from the moment you apply to the moment you get an answer, each step becomes a smaller problem that you can prepare for.

One honest note first. Hiring processes differ between companies, industries and countries. A large company that visits colleges hires in a very different way from a small workshop, a shop or an agency. What follows is the common pattern, not a rule. Always read the message you receive from the employer, because it usually tells you what to expect.
The usual stages

items: **Application.** You send your resume or CV, sometimes with a cover letter or a form. Many companies use software to read it first. A clear, plain resume helps here.

**Screening.** A recruiter or HR person checks your details by phone, video or message. They confirm that you meet the basic needs and ask simple questions: where you live, when you can start, what pay you expect, whether you can work in that country.
**Written or online test.** Common for larger employers and for technical and finance roles. It can test aptitude (numbers, logic, English), subject knowledge or coding.
**Interview rounds.** One to four conversations. They may be technical (the work itself), managerial (the person you would work for) and HR (fit, pay, rules).
**Offer and checks.** An offer, then document checks and sometimes a reference or background check, then a joining date.

content.text: Not every job has all of these. A shop assistant job might be one conversation on the same day. A campus placement drive might run a test, a group discussion and two interviews in a single day. A graduate scheme in the UK may have an online form, a video exercise and an assessment day that takes many weeks. Expect more steps for bigger employers and fewer for small ones.
What each round is really testing
Knowing the purpose of each stage helps you decide how to prepare.

items: **The screening call** tests whether you are reachable, clear and basically suitable. Be on time, speak clearly and have your facts ready. This stage removes many candidates who forgot to prepare for it.
**The test** checks a basic skill level at scale. It is usually about accuracy under time pressure, so practice with a timer.

**The technical or skills round** checks whether you can do the work or learn it. Interviewers know you are a fresher. They look for solid basics, honest answers and how you think when you do not know something.
**The managerial round** asks whether they would like to work with you every day. Attitude, curiosity and reliability matter a lot here.
**The HR round** checks fit, expectations and logistics: pay, notice period, location, the company rules. It is also a chance for you to ask your questions.

content.text: How it differs by country
These are general habits, not laws, and they change between companies.

items: **India.** Large employers often recruit through campus drives, with a written round, group discussion, technical interview and an HR interview. Questions about family background, marital status and similar topics sometimes come up. You may politely answer briefly and steer back to your skills. Notice periods and joining dates are discussed openly.

**United Kingdom.** Many employers use competency-based questions (“tell me about a time when...”) and ask about your right to work in the UK. Graduate employers often use online tests and assessment centres. Equality rules mean personal questions such as age or marital status should not be used in hiring decisions.

**Canada.** Behavioural questions are very common, and employers often ask for examples of teamwork and problem solving. Clear, direct answers and concrete examples are valued. Questions about age, family status or religion are not appropriate in hiring.

**African countries.** Practice varies widely between countries and sectors. Large companies and organisations often use written tests and panel interviews. Smaller firms may rely on one conversation and references from people they trust. Bring clear copies of your documents.

content.text: If anything in an interview makes you uncomfortable, such as being asked to pay a fee or share a bank password, stop. Lesson 14 explains how to spot fake job offers.
How long does it take?

There is no fixed time. Some small employers decide within a day. Large employers can take weeks or months, and sometimes never reply. Do not stop applying while you wait for one answer. A calm approach is to apply to several roles at once, keep a simple list of what you sent, when and to whom, and follow up politely after a week or two if they gave no date.
Types of interview formats

items: **One to one.** You and one interviewer. The most common format.
**Panel.** Two to five interviewers. Look at the person who asks the question, but include the others when you answer.
**Group interview or group discussion.** Several candidates together. They watch how you listen and contribute.
**Phone or video.** Common for screening. Lesson 12 covers how to set up well.
**Walk-in.** You arrive at a set time and wait your turn. Bring copies of documents and be ready for a quick conversation.

content.text: Your first checklist
Before you study any questions, set up the basics. These take an hour and remove many small worries.

items: Make sure your resume is clear and honest. You can build one with the [free resume builder](/app) on this site and check how software reads it with the [ATS checker](/features/ats-checker).
Write a list of the companies and roles you applied to, with dates.
Set up a professional email address and a phone voicemail message. Check them daily.
Prepare a folder, on your phone and on paper, with your certificates, ID, photos and copies of your resume.
Choose a quiet place and a time for phone calls.

content.text: An interview is a two-way conversation. The employer is also trying to win you. You are allowed to ask questions and to decide that a job is not right for you.
Your task

items: Write the stages you think the last job you applied for will use. Then check the job advert or message for clues.
List the people you could ask for a reference (a teacher, lecturer, previous manager or community leader) and ask their permission.
Create the document folder described above.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: You can name the usual five stages in order.
You know which stage you find hardest and can name one thing you will do about it.
Your documents and a copy of your resume are ready on paper and on your phone.

steps.say: You apply with a clear resume. Software or a person reads it first.
A short screening call or message confirms the basics.
Many employers add a written or online test to check basic skills.
You then meet one to four interviewers: technical, manager and HR.
If it goes well, you get an offer and document checks before the joining date.

faqs.q: How many interview rounds are normal for a fresher?
faqs.a: It varies. A small employer may hold one conversation. Larger employers often have a test and two or three interviews. Read the message from the employer for the exact steps.

faqs.q: Is it normal to be asked about marital status or family in an interview?
faqs.a: It happens in some places, but in many countries such questions should not be used in hiring. You can answer briefly and politely and return to your skills and availability.

lessons.title: Research the Company and the Role Before You Go
lessons.metaTitle: Research the Company Before an Interview
lessons.description: Learn quick, honest research: read the job advert closely, understand the company, find the skills they need and prepare your own questions.

content.text: Many fresh candidates walk into an interview knowing only the name of the company. Interviewers notice this immediately. The question “What do you know about us?” is common and easy to prepare for. One hour of good research makes you more confident, gives you better answers and shows you are serious about this job, not just any job.
Start with the job advert
The job advert is the best clue to what the employer wants. Read it slowly, twice. Then do this.

items: Copy the advert into a document so you do not lose it if the link disappears.
Underline every skill, tool and duty it mentions. These are the words the interviewer will use.
Split them into two groups: **must have** and **nice to have**. Adverts often list too many things. The first items and repeated items are usually the important ones.
Next to each must-have, write one real example from your life where you used or learned it: a college project, an internship, volunteer work, a part-time job, a course.

content.text: Now you have a map. For each key requirement, you already hold a short story. That story becomes your answer when the interviewer asks about it. It also shows you where you have gaps, so you can prepare an honest reply for them (lesson 8).

Do not claim skills you do not have. A fresher who says “I have not used that tool yet, but I have used a similar one and I learn quickly” is trusted more than someone who bluffs and is caught in the next question.
Learn about the company
You do not need to know everything. You need a few clear facts and your own thoughts about them. Look at these places.

items: **The company website.** Read the About page, the products or services, and any news or blog. Notice who their customers are.
**Their social media or LinkedIn page.** See what they share and how they describe themselves.
**Recent news.** Search for the company name with the word “news”. Look for something recent and positive, such as a new product, a new branch or an award.
**Company reviews.** On this site and elsewhere, employees sometimes describe working there. Read them carefully, remember that they are one person's view, and look for patterns.
**The people.** If you know who will interview you, look at their role. Never contact them in a way that feels intrusive.

content.text: Write five lines: what the company does, who it serves, how big it is (if you can tell), one recent thing you noticed, and one thing you like about it. This takes about twenty minutes and gives you material for “Tell me what you know about us” and “Why do you want to work here?”.
Understand the role in daily terms

A job title does not tell you what a person does all day. Try to picture a normal Tuesday in the role. What tasks will you do? Who will you work with? What does a good day look like? You can find clues in the advert, in descriptions of similar roles, and in the roadmap pages on this site, which explain typical steps and skills for many careers.

If you know someone who works in a similar role, ask them for ten minutes. Good questions are: What is a normal day like? What do you wish you had known when you started? What do new people struggle with? Say thank you, and do not ask for a job in the same breath.
Know the basics of the industry

A little background helps. If you apply to a bank, know what kind of customers a bank serves. If you apply to a hospital, understand the roles of the people around you. If you apply to a factory or workshop, be familiar with safety rules and shifts. For a technical role, read about the main tools in your field. You do not need to be an expert. You need to sound like someone who has taken an interest.
Prepare your own questions
Almost every interview ends with “Do you have any questions for us?”. Saying “No” sounds uninterested. Prepare three to five real questions, based on your research. Good examples:

items: “What would a successful first three months look like in this role?”
“How does the team work together day to day?”
“What training or support do new people receive?”
“What are the biggest challenges the team faces right now?”
“What are the next steps in the process?”

content.text: Avoid asking about pay, leave or perks as your first question. These matter, and you should learn about them, but they are better raised later, or when the interviewer brings them up (lesson 13).
A one-page prep sheet
Put what you learned on a single page you can read quickly before the interview.

COMPANY: what they do, who they serve, one recent fact
ROLE: three main tasks, three skills they ask for
MY EXAMPLES: one real story for each skill
GAPS: what I have not done yet and how I will learn it
QUESTIONS: 3 to 5 questions I will ask
LOGISTICS: place, time, who to ask for, phone number

Reading this page for ten minutes before you go is more helpful than a long night of panic study. Keep your prep sheets for each application. They are a record, and you can reuse parts for similar roles.
What not to do

items: Do not repeat the company's slogan as your answer. Say it in your own words.
Do not criticise a competitor or a previous employer.
Do not pretend to know more than you do. A sincere “I read that you are expanding into the city, and I would like to learn how that works” is better than a made-up opinion.
Do not rely on a single source. Read more than one.

content.text: Your task

items: Choose a real job advert. Mark the must-haves and write one real example from your life for each of the top five.
Write your five-line company summary, using the company's website and one news search.
Write three questions you would ask the interviewer.
Fill in the one-page prep sheet.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Every top requirement has a real example next to it, or a gap that you named honestly.
Your questions are about the job and team, not only about pay.
You can say in two sentences what the company does and why you want to work there.

steps.say: Read the job advert closely and mark the skills it asks for.
Find a few real facts about the company from its own website and recent news.
Match each key skill with one real example from your studies, work or projects.
Put the facts, examples, gaps and your questions on one page.
In the interview your answers are specific, and your questions show real interest.

faqs.q: How much research is enough?
faqs.a: About an hour is enough for most fresher roles. Read the job advert closely, learn what the company does, find one recent fact, and prepare a few questions.

faqs.q: What if I cannot find anything about a small company?
faqs.a: Use the job advert, the owner or team page if any, and ask the recruiter a few questions. Showing curiosity about a small business is itself a good sign.

lessons.title: Know Your Resume: Projects, Internships and Skills
lessons.metaTitle: Know Your Resume Before the Interview
lessons.description: Interviewers ask about everything on your resume. Learn to prepare each line, explain projects clearly and answer follow-up questions honestly.

content.text: Your resume is a list of promises. Every line says: ask me about this, I know it. Interviewers do exactly that. They pick something from your page and dig. “You wrote Excel. What is a pivot table?” “You listed a project on student attendance. What was your part in it?” Candidates who cannot explain their own resume lose trust fast. This lesson shows you how to prepare so that your own page becomes your biggest strength.
The rule: only write what you can explain

Go through your resume line by line. For each skill, tool, project and responsibility ask three questions. Can I explain it in two sentences? Can I give an example of using it? If the interviewer asks one more question, can I answer honestly? If the answer to any of these is no, either learn it before the interview or remove it. Our resume checker and templates push you to put real, checkable facts on the page, and not to pad it with keywords you cannot back up.
Being honest protects you. Exaggerated claims are easy to test in an interview, and on the job they can be found out later, which can cost you the role.
The three-part story for each project
Freshers often have more projects than jobs, so projects carry your resume. Prepare each one with this three-part story. It takes about a minute to say.

items: **The problem.** What was the project for? Who would use it? “We built a small app to help our college library track borrowed books.”
**Your part.** What did you personally do? Use “I”, not only “we”. “I designed the database tables and wrote the search page.”
**The result and the lesson.** What happened, and what did you learn? “It handled about 200 books in our test, and I learned how important it is to check user input.”

content.text: Only give numbers that are true. If you did not measure anything, do not invent a figure. Say what you observed instead: “Our teacher and four classmates tested it and found two bugs I then fixed.” That is believable and specific.
Then prepare for the follow-up questions every project invites.

items: What was the hardest part and how did you solve it?
What would you do differently now?
Why did you choose this tool or method?
How did you work with others? What if someone disagreed with you?
What happened when it did not work?

content.text: Internships, part-time jobs and volunteering

For each experience, be ready to describe what you did on a normal day, one thing you are proud of, one difficulty you solved, and what you learned about working with other people. Jobs that seem small, such as serving in a shop, helping in a family business or tutoring younger students, show reliability, patience, customer care and responsibility. These are things every employer wants. Do not apologise for them. Explain what they taught you.
Skills: prove each one
A skills list is the easiest part of a resume to challenge. Prepare a quick proof for each skill.

Skill: Microsoft Excel
Proof: Used it to track my family shop's weekly sales for six months;
       learned SUM, filters and a simple pivot table.

Skill: Python (basic)
Proof: Wrote a script that renamed 300 photos by date; finished a
       beginner course; can explain loops and functions.

Skill: Customer service
Proof: Worked weekends at a phone shop; handled returns and complaints.
When a skill is basic, say so with the level: “basic”, “working knowledge”, “comfortable”. Interviewers respect honest levels and will not expect you to be an expert in something you list as basic.
Education: be ready for details

Know your marks or grades, your main subjects, and why you chose your course. Be ready for questions about a low result or a failed subject. Answer calmly: what happened, what you did about it, what you learned. Blaming teachers or other people sounds weak, and a clear and brief explanation of what changed sounds strong.
Check the facts on the page
Small mistakes cause large doubts. Before every interview, check these things on the version you sent that employer.

items: Dates are correct and match your documents.
Names of companies, colleges and tools are spelled correctly.
Your phone number and email work. Call yourself from another phone to be sure.
Anything you claim, such as a certificate, can be shown if asked.
The resume is your latest version. Keep a copy of exactly what you sent each employer, because you might have tailored it.

content.text: If you want a clean starting point, build your resume with the [free tools on this site](/templates), then print it. The [ATS checker](/features/ats-checker) also shows you what a reading program can and cannot extract from your file, which is useful before you hit send.
Practise out loud

Reading in your head is not the same as speaking. Ask a friend or family member to pick any line from your resume and ask “Tell me about this”. Do it ten times. You will notice which lines you explain well and which make you stumble. Fix the stumbling ones with more practice or by changing the resume. Record yourself on your phone and listen once. Everyone dislikes their own voice, but it is the fastest way to catch “um”, “like” and very long answers.
Your task

items: Print your resume. Next to each project and skill, write the three-part story or the one-line proof.
Ask a friend to question you on three random lines for five minutes each. Note any line you struggled with.
Remove or fix any claim you could not support.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Every project has a problem, your part and a result written in your own words.
You can talk about each project for one minute without reading.
There is nothing on your resume that you would be embarrassed to be asked about.

animation.title: Every line can become a question

steps.say: Every line on your resume is something the interviewer may ask about.
For each line, you prepare a short true story: the problem, your part and the result.
The interviewer picks a line and asks you to tell more, or asks a follow-up question.
A clear, honest answer builds trust. A claim you cannot explain loses it quickly.

faqs.q: What if I have no projects or internships?
faqs.a: Use coursework, volunteering, family business help, part-time work, or a small project you do on your own. The lesson on having no experience shows how to talk about these honestly.

faqs.q: Should I remove skills I only know a little?
faqs.a: You can keep them if you mark the level honestly, such as basic, and you can explain what you have done with them. Remove anything you could not discuss for two minutes.

lessons.title: Tell Me About Yourself: A Simple Answer That Works
lessons.metaTitle: Tell Me About Yourself: Fresher Answer
lessons.description: Build a 60-second answer to the most common opening question using a clear structure: who you are, what you can do, and why this job. Made-up samples included.

content.text: “Tell me about yourself.” Almost every interview begins with it. It sounds friendly and open, which is exactly why candidates ramble, start from childhood or read their resume aloud. The interviewer is not asking for your life story. They want to know in about a minute: Who are you now? What can you do? Why are you here? A simple structure answers all three.
There is also a longer [guide on this question](/blog/tell-me-about-yourself-interview-answer) on this site. This lesson gives the practical method and lets you build and practise your own answer.
The three-part structure: Present, Past, Future

items: **Present.** Who are you right now? Your current studies or job, and what you are focused on.
**Past.** The two or three most relevant things you have done, such as projects, internships or skills, that connect to this role.
**Future.** Why you want this job and what you hope to do or learn there.

content.text: Keep it to about 60 to 90 seconds, which is roughly 150 to 200 words. A good answer ends with a clear link to the role, so the interviewer can ask their next question easily.
A made-up sample for a college graduate
The names and facts below are invented, to show the shape. Use your own true details.

"I'm Anjali, and I've just finished my B.Com at a college in Pune.
I enjoyed accounting and spreadsheets most. During my final year I
helped my uncle's hardware shop keep its monthly sales records in
Excel, which cut the time he spent on it each week. I also finished
a short online course in Tally basics. I'm looking for my first
role in accounts, and your junior accounts assistant job interested
me because it involves invoices and reconciliation, which are the
parts I enjoy. I want to learn how a larger team handles them."

Notice what this does. In the present, Anjali is a recent graduate. In the past, one concrete experience and one skill. In the future, she names the role and what she wants to learn. It has no exaggeration, and each sentence invites a follow-up question: “How did you set up the records?”
A made-up sample for a school leaver or skilled trade applicant

"My name is Samuel. I finished secondary school last year and
since then I've been helping my cousin, who is an electrician. I
can wire a room, fit sockets and switches, and I've learned to read
a simple circuit diagram. I have a safe working record and I'm
learning for my trade certificate. I'm applying here because you
are hiring a trainee electrician and I want to learn from a
company that does bigger installations."
Simple words, true facts, and a clear reason. Interviewers for practical roles care about reliability, safety and willingness to learn. This answer says all three without bragging.
What to include, what to leave out

items: **Include** facts that match the job: skills, studies, experience, an achievement.
**Include** one personal touch if it is natural and relevant, such as a hobby that shows teamwork or discipline. One line is enough.
**Leave out** your full life story, your age and family details, and anything that is not connected to the job.
**Leave out** negative comments about people or places.
**Leave out** things you cannot discuss in more detail if asked.

content.text: Common mistakes

items: Starting with “My name is...” and then reading your resume in order. The interviewer has already read it.
Being too long. After two minutes, people stop listening.
Being too short: “I am a hard-working fresher.” That gives them nothing to work with.
Using the same answer for every job without changing the last part.
Memorising word for word. It sounds stiff and you panic if you forget a line. Memorise the three parts and a few key facts instead.

content.text: How to build your own answer

items: Write the present in one sentence: who you are and what you are doing now.
Choose two things from the past that fit this job. Write one sentence each, with a real detail.
Write the future in one or two sentences: why this role and what you want to learn.
Read it aloud and time it. Cut to 60 to 90 seconds.
Practise with three versions of the ending for three different jobs.

content.text: For example, a template you can fill in:

"I'm [name]. I [studied / worked / trained] in [subject or field]
and I'm currently [what you do now].
Recently I [one concrete thing you did] and I [second thing / skill].
I'm interested in this [role] because [one honest reason linked to
the job], and I'd like to [what you want to learn or contribute]."
Special cases

items: **Career gap.** Mention it briefly in the past part if it matters, with what you did or learned, then move on. The lesson on gaps and having no experience gives wording.
**Career change.** In the past part, explain the skills you bring from your earlier work, and say why you chose this new direction.
**Nervous?** Slow down and breathe before you start. A calm first sentence sets the tone for the whole interview.
**Online interview.** Look at the camera, and keep your notes out of view, with a few key words only.

content.text: Your task

items: Write your own present, past and future answer using the template and keep it under 200 words.
Say it aloud while timing yourself. Aim for 60 to 90 seconds.
Change only the last sentence for two different jobs.
Say it to one person and ask: What would you ask me next?

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The answer takes 60 to 90 seconds and contains no untrue claims.
Each part has at least one concrete detail.
Your listener could name your main strength afterwards.

steps.say: Start with the present: who you are and what you are doing now, in one sentence.
Move to the past: two real things that fit this job, with one concrete detail each.
Finish with the future: why this role, and what you want to learn there.
In about 60 to 90 seconds you have given the interviewer an easy next question.

faqs.q: How long should my answer to tell me about yourself be?
faqs.a: About 60 to 90 seconds, or roughly 150 to 200 words. Long enough to give facts, short enough to keep attention.

faqs.q: Should I mention my family or hobbies?
faqs.a: Keep the focus on the job. One short, natural line about a hobby that shows a useful quality is fine. Leave out family details unless they are directly relevant.

lessons.title: Strengths and Weaknesses: Honest Answers Without Cliches
lessons.description: Answer the strengths and weaknesses questions with real examples and honest, safe weaknesses. Learn what to avoid and how to show progress.

content.text: Two questions come up in a huge number of interviews: “What are your strengths?” and “What is your biggest weakness?”. They seem simple, but they are easy to answer badly. Candidates say “I am hard-working and a perfectionist” and everyone in the room has heard it a hundred times. This lesson shows a better way: choose honestly, use a small example, and show how you work on it.
Strengths: say it, then prove it

A strength is only believable with evidence. A claim alone (“I am a good team player”) is weak. A claim with a short example is strong. Use this pattern: **the strength, a short example, why it matters for this job**.

Weak:   "I am very hard-working and a quick learner."

Better: "I learn new tools quickly. In my final year I had two weeks
        to learn basic SQL for a project, and I finished with a
        working report. In this role you'll use new software often,
        so I think that will help."
How do you choose which strengths to talk about? Look at your prep sheet from lesson 2. Pick two or three strengths that match the job's top requirements and that you can support with real examples.
Ideas for fresher strengths
Pick what is true for you. Here are some real strengths that employers value, with the kind of evidence you can give.

items: **Learning fast.** You picked up a tool, language or process in a short time. Say what and how long.
**Reliability.** You never missed a shift or deadline in a job or project. Say for how long.
**Teamwork.** You worked with others and helped finish a group project. Say what your role was.
**Communication.** You explained things to customers, classmates or younger students.
**Attention to detail.** You found mistakes in a report, a count or a design before they caused problems.
**Problem solving.** You faced a problem and worked out a way through it.
**Responsibility.** You looked after a shop, a younger sibling or a group's money. Real life counts.

content.text: Weaknesses: be honest, be safe, show progress

Interviewers do not ask this to catch you out. They want to know whether you know yourself, whether you can be honest, and whether you work on improving. A good weakness answer has three parts: **a real, small weakness, what you do about it, and the progress you have seen**.

"I used to get nervous speaking in front of groups and avoided it.
I knew that would hold me back, so in college I volunteered to present
in two classes. It's still not my favourite thing, but I now prepare
a short outline and practise once aloud, and my last presentation
went well. I'm still working on it."
This answer is honest (it names a real weakness), safe (public speaking is not a core requirement for most entry-level roles) and shows action and progress. It also sounds like a real person.
Choose a safe weakness

A safe weakness is real, is not essential to the job, and can be improved. Examples: nervousness when speaking, being new to a particular tool, taking on too much and having to learn to prioritise, finding it hard to say no to extra requests, or finding it hard to ask for help at first.
Avoid these.

items: **Cliches.** “I'm a perfectionist” or “I work too hard”. They sound like a trick and interviewers dislike them.
**Weaknesses that hurt the role.** Saying you are always late when applying to a job that needs punctuality, or that you cannot work in a team for a team role.
**Blaming others.** “My weakness is that other people are lazy.”
**Saying you have none.** Everyone has areas to improve.

content.text: Say what you do about it

The most important part is what you do. Name a specific habit, tool or action. “I use a to-do list and check it twice a day” beats “I am working on it”. If you have only started, say so: “I am only beginning, but I have started...”.
Related questions

items: **“What is your biggest achievement?”** Use the same pattern as strengths: the situation, what you did, the result. It does not need to be big. A fresher's real achievement can be finishing a hard course, a project or helping a team win a college event.
**“How would your friends or teachers describe you?”** Choose a quality and add a short example. Use words that someone would really say about you.
**“What do you do when you do not know something?”** Honest answer: you try to find out first (documentation, notes, searching), then you ask a colleague, and you note it down for next time.

content.text: Practise the delivery

Say your answers aloud. Keep strengths to one or two sentences plus an example. Keep the weakness answer to about thirty seconds. Smile naturally and speak at a normal pace. If an interviewer follows up (“And how is that going?”), give a short true update. You will sound confident because you are being honest.
If you cannot think of examples, ask a friend, a teacher or a family member: “When have you seen me do something well?” You may be surprised by what they remember.
Your task

items: Choose two strengths from your prep sheet and write one real example for each, using the strength-example-relevance pattern.
Choose one safe weakness and write the three parts: the weakness, what you do, the progress.
Write one answer to “What is your biggest achievement?”.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Each strength has a small true example attached.
Your weakness is real, not a cliche, and you can describe one action you have taken.
You can say each answer aloud in under a minute.

steps.say: Name one real strength that fits the job, such as learning new tools quickly.
Back it with a short example: what you did, in what time and with what result.
Link it to the job so the interviewer sees why it helps them.
An answer with proof sounds believable. A list of adjectives does not.

faqs.q: What is a good weakness to say in an interview?
faqs.a: Choose a real weakness that is not essential to the job, such as nervousness speaking to groups or being new to a tool, and explain what you are doing to improve it.

faqs.q: Is it bad to say I am a perfectionist?
faqs.a: It is a cliche that most interviewers have heard many times and often find unconvincing. A specific, honest weakness with an action plan is more credible.

lessons.title: Why Do You Want This Job? Why Should We Hire You?
lessons.metaTitle: Why This Job? Why Should We Hire You?
lessons.description: Answer the two big motivation questions with honest, specific reasons. Learn to link your skills to the employer needs without bragging.

content.text: After the opening, interviewers usually test your motivation with two questions: “Why do you want to work here?” and “Why should we hire you?”. They are the same question from two sides. The first asks what draws you to the company. The second asks what you bring to it. Both are chances to show that you did your homework (lesson 2) and that you understand what the employer needs.
Why do you want to work here?

A weak answer talks only about you: “I need a job” or “It is a big company with a good salary”. These may be true, but they give the employer no reason to choose you. A strong answer has two parts: something real about the company or the role, and how it matches something you care about or want to learn.

Weak:   "I want a job in IT and your company is well known."

Better: "I've followed your work on school management software. I did
        a small project for my college's attendance, so I can see
        how much time good software saves teachers. I'd like to
        learn how a professional team builds that kind of product."
The better answer shows a real link (the attendance project), real interest (school software) and a learning goal (how a team builds it). The reasons are honest. They do not need to be dramatic.
Where do honest reasons come from?

items: **The work itself.** The tasks in the advert match what you enjoy or are good at.
**What you can learn.** Training, tools, mentors or kinds of customers you want to meet.
**The company's product or mission.** Something real that you noticed in your research.
**Location and practical fit.** Distance, shifts or hours that you can sustain. This is a valid reason when stated politely and not as the only one.
**Growth.** A path from trainee to a more senior role, if the company has described one.

content.text: It is fine to also need the income. You do not have to hide that you need a job. Just do not make it the only reason. Pair it with a reason that is about the work.
Why should we hire you?

This question can feel like asking you to boast. Think of it as a short summary: **what the job needs, what you have, and the proof**. You are connecting your best two or three matches from the prep sheet to the employer's top needs.

"From your advert I understand you need someone who can handle
customer calls calmly and keep accurate records. I worked weekends
at a phone shop for a year, where I handled returns and complaints
and kept the daily sales sheet, which my manager checked and found
correct. I'm also quick to learn new software. I think that
combination would help me do well in this role quickly."
Notice that it does not compare you to other candidates, and it does not claim you are the best. You cannot know who else applied. Say what you offer and why it fits.
A simple formula

items: **Need.** Say what you understand the job requires.
**Match.** Tell the interviewer two things you have that fit.
**Proof.** Give one short real example.
**Close.** One sentence about how this would help the team.

content.text: Related questions you may meet

items: **“What do you know about our company?”** Use the five lines from your research. Mention what they do, who they serve and one recent fact.

**“Where do you see yourself in five years?”** Interviewers want to see ambition that fits the role. An honest answer sounds like: “I would like to have grown into a confident member of the team, taking on more responsibility, and learning skills such as ... ”. Avoid naming a job at the company that is far above the role. Avoid saying that you will probably leave.
**“Why did you choose this career or course?”** Tell the true story in a few sentences: what interested you, what you did to find out more, what you enjoy.
**“What other jobs are you applying for?”** You can say you are looking at similar roles in the same field, without naming other companies. Be honest, and say this role is a strong interest.

content.text: Avoid these answers

items: Answers that could be said about any company. If you could swap the company's name and the answer still works, it is too general.
Saying money is the main reason. You may be paid for your work, but employers prefer people who care about the job as well.
Criticising a previous employer, college or teacher.
Over-flattery. “It is the best company in the world” sounds fake. Be specific and sincere instead.

content.text: If you honestly do not know much about the company, say so in a positive way: “I have only had a few days to learn about you, but what I have found is X. I would like to learn more.” Then ask a good question. Honest curiosity works better than pretending.
Your task

items: Write your answer to “Why do you want to work here?” for one real company, using one fact from your research and one reason that is about you.
Write your answer to “Why should we hire you?” using the need, match, proof and close pattern.
Write an honest, short answer to “Where do you see yourself in five years?”.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Your answers mention something specific that could not be said about every company.
Your hire-you answer has one real example and does not compare you with other people.
None of your answers criticises anyone.

steps.say: Start with what the job needs, using the words from the advert.
Say two things you have that match that need.
Give one short, true example as proof.
Finish with one sentence on how this would help the team.

faqs.q: Is it wrong to say I need the job?
faqs.a: No. Many people need income. Just do not make it your only reason. Add something specific about the work, the company or what you want to learn.

faqs.q: How do I answer where I see myself in five years?
faqs.a: Describe growth that fits the role, such as becoming confident, taking on more responsibility and learning specific skills. Avoid naming a far higher job or saying you plan to leave.

lessons.title: Behavioural Questions and the STAR Method
lessons.description: Answer questions that start with "Tell me about a time when..." using the STAR method. Includes made-up samples, example questions and fresher-friendly stories.

content.text: “Tell me about a time when you worked in a team.” “Describe a situation where you handled a difficult customer.” These are **behavioural questions**, and they are standard in many UK and Canadian interviews and increasingly in India and across Africa. The idea is simple: past behaviour is a good guide to future behaviour. So instead of asking what you would do, the interviewer asks what you did.

Freshers often say: “I have no work experience, so I have nothing to say.” This is not true. You have stories from college, projects, sports, volunteering, family work and part-time jobs. This lesson shows you how to find them and tell them clearly with the STAR method.
What is STAR?
STAR is a way to organise a story in four short parts.

items: **S: Situation.** Set the scene in one or two sentences. Where were you, and what was happening?
**T: Task.** What was your job or the problem to solve?
**A: Action.** What did you do? This is the longest part. Use “I”, and say what you personally did and why.
**R: Result.** What happened? Add what you learned. If you can, say what you would do differently.

content.text: A good STAR answer takes one to two minutes. The most common mistake is spending too long on the situation and too little on the action and result.
A made-up sample: teamwork
Question: “Tell me about a time you worked in a team.” The story below is invented to show the shape.

S: "In my final year, four of us had to build a mini-project for our
   database course. One teammate stopped replying a week before the
   deadline."
T: "I was the group's coordinator, so I had to make sure we still
   delivered."
A: "I messaged him and he said he was struggling with a family issue.
   I asked what part he could still do, and he agreed to write the test
   cases. I took over his coding part and split the rest between the two
   others. I also set up a shared checklist so we could all see what was
   left."
R: "We submitted on time and got a good grade. I learned that asking
   what someone can do works better than blaming, and I now check in
   with the team earlier."
The story is honest, ordinary and specific. There is no hero speech. Notice the action: it shows communication, kindness and organisation, qualities teams like.
Another made-up sample: a difficult customer

S: "I worked weekends at a mobile accessories shop. One Saturday a
   customer came back angry because a charger had stopped working."
T: "I had to help him without a long argument, and follow the shop's
   return rule."
A: "I listened without interrupting, apologised that it hadn't worked,
   checked the receipt and the warranty, and offered a replacement as
   the rule allowed. I explained how to check the cable too."
R: "He thanked me and bought a case. My manager said the way I handled
   it was good. I learned to stay calm and let people finish talking."
Common behavioural questions for freshers

items: Tell me about a time you worked in a team.
Describe a time you had a disagreement with someone. What happened?
Tell me about a time you made a mistake. What did you do?
Give an example of a time you had to learn something quickly.
Tell me about a time you met a tight deadline.
Describe a time you helped someone.
Tell me about a time you took the lead.
Describe a goal you set and how you reached it.
Tell me about a time you handled pressure or a lot of tasks at once.

content.text: Build a story bank

You do not need a new story for each question. Prepare five to seven good stories, and a story can answer several questions if you shift the emphasis. A group project story can answer teamwork, leadership, conflict and deadline questions.

items: List ten moments from college, work, volunteering, sports, hobbies or family life where something happened and you did something. Include moments that did not go well.
Choose the five to seven that show your qualities best and that you can explain in detail.
Write each as a short STAR outline of four lines.
Beside each, write which questions it could answer.
Practise telling each in under two minutes.

content.text: Stories about mistakes and failures

Interviewers ask about mistakes because they want to see honesty, responsibility and learning. A good answer: you own the mistake, you fix it, you learn. A bad answer: you blame others, or pretend you never made one. Pick a mistake that is real but not serious, and make the Result part about what you changed.
Tips for telling the story

items: Say what **you** did. Even in a team story, interviewers need to know your contribution.
Keep names out. Say “a teammate” instead of using real names, to be polite.
Avoid exaggeration. A small, true story is better than a huge claim.
Finish with what you learned. It shows you grow from experience.
It is fine to pause and think. “That is a good question. Let me think of an example” is a natural thing to say.

content.text: In some countries, including the UK and Canada, interviewers may score your answer against a fixed checklist, so being specific and complete matters. In other places, the interview is more of a conversation. The STAR method works well in both.
Your task

items: Write six moments in your life where you did something useful. Choose four and write them as short STAR outlines.
Practise one aloud and time it. Cut it to under two minutes.
Write one honest mistake story with a clear lesson.
Match each story to at least two questions from the list.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Each story has all four parts, and the Action part is the longest.
You used “I” for your own actions.
You have at least five stories ready.

steps.say: Situation: set the scene in one or two sentences, where and when.
Task: say what your job or problem was in that situation.
Action: explain what you personally did and why. This is the longest part.
Result: what happened, what you learned, and what you would change.

faqs.q: What if I have no work experience for STAR stories?
faqs.a: Use college projects, group work, sports, volunteering, part-time jobs and family responsibilities. Interviewers expect freshers to use these.

faqs.q: How long should a STAR answer be?
faqs.a: About one to two minutes. Spend most of the time on the Action and the Result.

lessons.title: No Experience, a Gap or a Career Change: Honest Answers
lessons.metaTitle: No Experience, Gaps, Career Change Answers
lessons.description: How to answer the hard questions: "You have no experience", "Why is there a gap?", "Why change careers?", low marks and a failed subject.

content.text: Almost everyone has something they worry the interviewer will ask about. You may have no work experience. You may have taken a break for health, family, money or because you could not find a job. Maybe your marks were low in one year. Maybe you are changing careers. The good news is that these are normal, interviewers have heard them before, and the way you answer matters more than the fact itself.
This lesson gives you a calm approach and sample wording for each. The samples are made up to show the shape, so use your own true facts. Never invent an explanation.
The calm formula for any hard question

items: **Acknowledge it simply.** Do not argue or get defensive. “Yes, that is right.”
**Give a short, honest reason.** One or two sentences. You do not owe more private detail than you want to share.
**Show what you did meanwhile.** Learning, working, caring, building.
**Return to the present and the job.** End by connecting to why you are ready now.

content.text: Practise saying it aloud, because the tone matters as much as the words. Aim for calm and matter-of-fact.
“You have no experience”
This is the most common challenge for freshers. Do not apologise. Instead, say what you do have: learning, projects, relevant practice, and enthusiasm to learn.

"That's true, I haven't had a full-time job in this field yet. What I
do have is two projects and a course in it, and I helped my family's
shop with its accounts for two years. I learn quickly and I'm
looking for a place to build real experience, and your trainee
programme looked like a good place to do that."

Practical ideas to build evidence before the interview: do a small project, volunteer for a local organisation, take a short course and finish it, help a small business with a real task, or contribute to a group effort. Even one or two real things change the conversation.

There is a full guide for resumes with no experience on this site, called [fresher resume with no experience](/blog/fresher-resume-no-experience), which helps you present these things on paper as well.
An employment gap

A gap is time between jobs or studies. Employers see gaps for many reasons. Health, family care, moving, a business that closed, searching for work, or study. They are mainly worried about two things: Are you reliable? Are your skills still current? Answer both.

"After my diploma I took about a year out to look after my
father while he recovered from surgery. During that time I kept my
skills fresh by taking an online bookkeeping course and doing
the accounts for a neighbour's shop. He's recovered well, and I'm
ready to work full time."

items: State the reason briefly. You do not have to share medical or family details.
Say what you did to stay active or learn, if anything. If you did nothing formal, caring for someone or searching for work is real work, and you can say so.
Say you are ready now, and give your availability.
Do not lie about dates to hide a gap. Dates are easy to check.

content.text: More ideas are in our guide to [explaining an employment gap](/blog/how-to-explain-employment-gap-on-resume).
A career change
Interviewers will ask: why leave a field where you have experience? Show that your move is a thought-out decision and that your old skills carry over.

"I worked for three years in retail, mainly in customer service and
stock control. I became interested in data when I started tracking
our sales on a spreadsheet. I've since done an Excel and SQL course
and a small analysis project. The customer knowledge and attention
to accuracy from retail fits this analyst role, and I'm ready to
start on a junior level."

items: Name the old skills that carry over, such as customer care, accuracy, planning and teamwork.
Show steps you took to learn the new field.
Be ready to accept a more junior start. Saying you understand this shows realism.

content.text: See also our [career change guide](/blog/career-change-resume-guide).
Low marks or a failed subject
Do not blame teachers or bad luck. Say what happened simply, what you did, and what changed.

"I did poorly in my second year because I was working part-time
and not managing my time well. I failed one subject and passed it on
the retake. After that I made a weekly plan, and my marks in the
final year were much better."
Interviewers like to see that you learn from setbacks. If you have more recent results or projects that show your ability, point to them.
Being asked something you cannot answer

Sometimes you simply do not know the answer. It is normal. Stay calm and say so honestly: “I haven't come across that. Here is how I would find out ...”. Then describe your approach: who you would ask, what you would read, what you would test. Interviewers are often more interested in how you think than in a memorised fact.
Questions you may be asked that are not appropriate

Some interviewers ask about age, marriage, children, religion, health or family plans. In many countries, including the UK and Canada, these should not influence hiring, and asking can be against the law. In others, it is common for personal questions to be asked. You have choices. You can answer briefly and move on. You can politely redirect: “I'm happy to talk about my availability and how I would manage the job.” Or you can decline to answer. Choose what feels right and safe for you.

If you feel you are being treated unfairly, remember that you can leave an interview, and that you can report serious concerns to the relevant authority in your country. You do not have to accept disrespect to get a job.
Your task

items: Write short honest answers for the questions that worry you most from the list above.
Check each answer for the four parts: acknowledge, short reason, what you did meanwhile, return to the present.
Say each aloud until it sounds calm. Time it. Each should be under 45 seconds.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Your answers are true and use no invented reasons.
None of them blames anyone else.
Each ends by returning to why you are ready now.

steps.say: A hard question comes up, such as a gap or no experience. Stay calm.
Acknowledge it simply and give a short, honest reason.
Say what you did in that time, such as learning, work or caring for someone.
Return to the present: you are ready now and here is why you fit the job.

faqs.q: Should I hide a gap on my resume?
faqs.a: Do not falsify dates. Be brief and honest, and say what you did in that time. Many employers care more about whether your skills are current than about the gap itself.

faqs.q: How do I answer a personal question I think is inappropriate?
faqs.a: You can answer briefly, politely steer back to your skills and availability, or decline to answer. Choose what feels right to you.

lessons.title: Aptitude and Written Tests: How to Prepare
lessons.description: Prepare for numerical, verbal and logical tests with a simple weekly plan, timing habits and calm test-day tactics. No tricks, just practice.

content.text: Many large employers, campus drives and graduate schemes start with a written or online test. You may see it called an aptitude test, a screening test, a psychometric test or an online assessment. The reason is simple: when thousands of people apply, a test is a fast, fair-looking way to reduce the list. This lesson tells you what these tests usually contain and how to prepare in a sensible way.

A note first. Do not pay anyone who promises you a pass or sells leaked papers. They are scams or cheating, and the second can end your career before it starts. Real preparation is free or cheap and takes steady practice.
What is usually tested

items: **Numerical ability.** Percentages, ratios, averages, simple interest, profit and loss, time and work, reading tables and charts.
**Verbal ability.** Reading short passages and answering questions, grammar, synonyms and antonyms, sentence correction, filling gaps.
**Logical reasoning.** Number and letter series, patterns, coding and decoding, puzzles, seating arrangements, statements and conclusions.
**Subject or technical questions.** Basics of your degree or the job, such as accounting, programming, engineering or computer basics.
**Situational judgement.** Short workplace situations where you choose the best response, used often by UK employers.
**Typing or computer skills tests** for office roles, and **trade or practical tests** for skilled jobs.

content.text: The test described in the job advert or invitation is the one that matters. Look for the name of the test provider and the topics. If the message does not say, ask the recruiter politely what to expect.
Know the format
Before you study, learn how the test works.

items: How many questions and how long? This tells you the time per question.
Is there negative marking, meaning points lost for wrong answers? If so, guessing carefully matters.
Can you go back to earlier questions, or is it one question at a time?
Is it on a computer or paper? A calculator allowed or not?
Is there a section cut-off, meaning a minimum score in each section?

content.text: Time per question is the key number. A test with 30 questions in 30 minutes gives you about a minute each. Some questions take 20 seconds, so you can spend longer on harder ones, but you must learn to leave a question and move on.
A four-week plan
A little each day beats a long study night. About 45 minutes a day is a good rhythm.

items: **Week 1: Basics.** Revisit the school-level topics: percentages, fractions, ratios and averages. Revise grammar rules. Take one short test to see where you are.
**Week 2: Topic practice.** Spend two days on each topic, with untimed practice at first, then timed sets of ten questions. Keep a notebook of mistakes.
**Week 3: Speed.** Do mixed timed sets. Learn shortcuts that you understand, not ones you memorise without meaning.
**Week 4: Full mock tests.** Take full-length timed tests, at the real time of day if possible. Review every wrong answer.

content.text: Habits that raise your score

items: **Keep an error log.** Write every mistake and why it happened: a calculation slip, not reading carefully, not knowing the method. Review the log each weekend.
**Learn to estimate.** In a numbers question, rounding to nearby values often shows which option is right.
**Read the question twice.** Many wrong answers come from missing the word “not” or the units.
**Skip and return.** If a question takes too long, mark it and move on. Easy marks wait later in the paper.
**Practise mental maths.** Times tables up to 20 and common fractions as percentages (one eighth is 12.5 per cent) save time.
**Read English daily.** A newspaper article or a news website for 15 minutes a day builds speed for verbal passages.

content.text: Good practice sources

Use free and low-cost resources and avoid paying large amounts. Past-paper style questions from your college, reputable free practice websites, school textbooks for the maths basics, and free mock tests offered by many employers and test providers themselves, which show you the real interface. Practise on the kind of device you will use.
Test-day tactics

items: Sleep and eat before the test. A tired brain makes silly mistakes.
Arrive early, or log in early for online tests, and check your internet and device.
Bring what is needed: ID, pens, a calculator if allowed, and a watch.
Read the instructions fully before starting the timer.
Do the questions you know first. Keep an eye on the clock.
If there is negative marking, only guess when you can remove at least one or two options.
In the last minutes, check that every question has an answer, unless guessing costs marks.

content.text: If you feel a panic wave, close your eyes for five seconds, breathe out slowly, and restart with the next question. One bad question does not decide your result.
Typing and computer skills tests

Office roles may test typing speed and accuracy and basic Word and Excel tasks. Practise typing with free tools for ten minutes a day. Focus on accuracy first, then speed. Learn basic Excel tasks such as sum, sort and filter. Our Excel course on this site is a good place to start.
Practical and trade tests

For skilled trades, the test may be practical: wiring a board, welding a joint, using a machine or reading a drawing. Safety comes first in these tests. Show that you check safety, use tools correctly and keep the work area tidy. Ask if you do not understand an instruction. Doing it slowly and safely beats doing it fast and unsafe.
If you do not pass a test, you can try again with other employers, and you will already know the format. Many successful candidates failed several tests first. Review your error log and keep going.
Your task

items: Choose the next test you expect to take. Find out the format: number of questions, time, negative marking.
Make a four-week plan with 45 minutes a day. Write the days and topics on a calendar.
Start an error log in a notebook. Add every mistake from your first practice set.
Take one timed practice set and calculate the time per question.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: You know the time per question for your test.
Your error log has at least ten entries with a reason for each.
You have booked time each day for practice.

steps.say: First learn the format: the number of questions, the time and whether wrong answers lose marks.
Practise a little each day with timed sets of questions.
Write each mistake and its reason in an error log, and review the log each week.
Finish with full timed mock tests, and review every wrong answer.

faqs.q: How long should I prepare for an aptitude test?
faqs.a: About four weeks at 45 minutes a day suits many people. Start earlier if the basics such as percentages and grammar feel weak.

faqs.q: Is it worth paying for leaked papers or a guaranteed pass?
faqs.a: No. These are usually scams, and using leaked papers is cheating. Real preparation uses free or low-cost practice and steady review.

lessons.title: The Technical Round: Basics, Projects and Thinking Aloud
lessons.metaTitle: Technical Interview Round: How to Prepare
lessons.description: Prepare for the technical interview as a fresher: know the basics, explain your projects, think aloud and handle questions you cannot answer.

content.text: The technical round is where an interviewer checks that you can do the work, or learn it. It could be about programming, accounting, electrical wiring, customer support tools, design, laboratory methods or machine operation. The subject changes. The pattern stays the same: they test your basics, your projects and the way you think. Freshers are not expected to know everything. They are expected to know the basics well and to be honest and curious.
What interviewers look for in a fresher

items: **Strong basics.** Not tricks. The core ideas from your degree or training, explained clearly.
**Your own work.** Evidence that you have used what you learned: projects, practicals, a workshop, a lab.
**Clear thinking.** How you approach a problem, even if you do not reach the answer.
**Honesty.** Saying “I don't know” and then reasoning, instead of guessing wildly.
**Willingness to learn.** Interest in the field outside class, such as reading, tools you tried, small experiments.

content.text: Prepare the basics properly

Go back to the main topics of your subject and the job advert. For each topic, you should be able to explain it simply, give an example, and say where it is used. Explaining to a friend or a younger student is a strong test. If you cannot explain a topic simply, you have not fully learned it yet.

Use a short list. Choose 15 to 25 core topics for the role. For a software role they could be variables and loops, functions, object-oriented ideas, a database basic, how the web works and one language in depth. For an accounts role: the accounting equation, debit and credit, journal and ledger, bank reconciliation and common spreadsheet functions. For an electrical or mechanical trade role: safety rules, tools, reading drawings, basic measurements and common faults. Revise one topic a day and say it aloud.
Depth beats breadth. Knowing eight topics deeply is better than knowing thirty at name level. If you say you know a topic, expect a second and third question on it.
Explain your projects

Your resume projects are the most likely start of a technical conversation. Prepare them as in lesson 3, and also prepare the technical side: the tools you used and why, the design in simple terms, the part you found hardest, what you would improve, and how you tested that it worked. If you used a framework or tutorial, say so honestly, and be clear about what you built yourself.
Think aloud
When you get a problem, say what you are thinking. Silence is hard for an interviewer to judge. This is especially true for coding or calculation questions. A good pattern:

items: **Repeat the problem** in your own words to be sure you understand. Ask a clarifying question if needed.
**Give a simple example** to show you understand: “If the input is 3 and 5, the answer should be ...”.
**Start with an obvious approach**, even if it is not the best, and say it.
**Work through it step by step** while talking. If you hit a wall, say so and try a different angle.
**Check your answer** with your example, and think of edge cases, such as an empty list or zero.
**Say how you could improve it** if you have time.

content.text: Interviewers like candidates who stay calm, ask good questions and correct their own mistakes. That matters more than a flawless answer.
Coding and technical exercises

For programming roles, you may get a coding exercise on paper, on a whiteboard, in a browser or as a take-home task. Practise on small problems regularly in the language you list. Free practice sites exist for this. Start with simple loops and strings, then lists and dictionaries, then basic searching and sorting ideas. Type the code yourself rather than reading solutions. After you solve a problem, ask what edge cases you missed.

For take-home tasks, read the instructions carefully, keep the solution clear and simple, add a short README on how to run it, and submit before the deadline. Do not copy another person's solution. Interviewers often ask you to explain every line.
When you do not know the answer
It will happen. Here is a calm way to handle it.

items: Say honestly: “I'm not sure about that.”
Share what you do know that is related: “I know how X works, so I think Y may be similar.”
Reason aloud to a sensible guess, and mark it as a guess.
If you are stuck, ask for a hint. It is a normal thing to do, and how you use the hint is informative.
Afterwards, look up the answer and add it to your notes. The same question may come back.

content.text: Never invent a confident wrong answer. A wrong answer said confidently is worse than an honest “I don't know, but here's how I would find out”.
Practical and trade interviews

For hands-on roles you may be asked about a job you did: “Tell me how you would fix a motor that won't start” or “What do you check before using this machine?”. Answer in order, in plain words, starting with safety. If you have worked on real equipment, describe it. If not, describe how you learned and what you practised.
Ask a good question at the end
A thoughtful technical question shows interest: “What tools does the team use day to day?” or “What would I learn in the first month?”. It is a chance to show you think about the work.
Your task

items: List 15 to 25 core topics for the role you want. Mark each one as strong, medium or weak.
Pick three weak ones and spend a week turning them to strong. Explain each aloud to someone.
Write the technical summary for each of your projects: tools, design, hardest part, testing, improvement.
Practise one problem aloud, using the six-step thinking-aloud method.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: You can explain every item on your topic list in simple words.
You have a technical summary of each project that you can say in two minutes.
You have a calm plan for a question you cannot answer.

steps.say: Repeat the problem in your own words, and ask a question if anything is unclear.
Give a small example to show you understand what is wanted.
Start with an obvious approach and explain each step as you go.
Check it against your example and edge cases, then say how you could improve it.

faqs.q: What if I do not know the answer in a technical interview?
faqs.a: Say so honestly, share what you do know that is related, and reason aloud. Asking for a hint is acceptable. Never invent a confident wrong answer.

faqs.q: How much should a fresher know?
faqs.a: Interviewers expect solid basics and your own projects, not expert knowledge. Depth on the core topics matters more than a long list of names.

lessons.title: Group Discussions and Case Questions
lessons.metaTitle: Group Discussion and Case Questions Tips
lessons.description: Do well in group discussions and case-style questions: how to start, listen, add value, handle loud people and structure a short problem-solving answer.

content.text: Some employers, especially large companies and campus drives, put several candidates in one room and give them a topic to discuss. This is a **group discussion**, or GD. Others ask a short business problem, called a **case question** or a guesstimate. Both look at the same things: how you think, how you speak, and how you behave with other people. You do not have to be the loudest person to do well. You have to be clear, respectful and useful.
What observers watch in a group discussion

items: **Content.** Do your points make sense and show you thought about the topic?
**Communication.** Is your speech clear, and do you stay on the topic?
**Listening.** Do you respond to what others say, and not just wait to talk?
**Teamwork.** Do you include quiet people and help the group reach a point?
**Behaviour.** Are you calm, polite and confident without being aggressive?

content.text: Notice that talking the most is not on the list. Candidates who shout and interrupt are usually marked down. Candidates who say fewer, better points, listen and summarise, often score higher.
Before you speak: take a few moments

When the topic is given, use the first minute to write two or three ideas. Think of the topic from several angles, which you can remember with this checklist: **people** (who is affected), **money** (costs and benefits), **society**, **technology**, **time** (short and long term) and **risks**. Even one point from each angle gives you material for the whole discussion.
A simple plan for the discussion

items: **Start well, if you can.** A good opening gives a short definition or context and one main point. “Social media is used by most young people. I think the key question is how to get its benefits while reducing the harm.” A clear start earns credit. But do not rush if you are not ready. A thoughtful second or third contribution is also fine.
**Add one new point each time.** Do not repeat what others said. Build on it: “Building on what Ravi said about schools, I'd add that ...”.
**Use examples.** A real example makes your point stronger than a general claim. Avoid made-up statistics. If you do not know a number, do not invent one.
**Include others.** If someone has been quiet, say: “We haven't heard from Meena. What do you think?”. It shows leadership.
**Redirect gently if the group drifts.** “We are talking about cost. Let's return to the main question.”
**Summarise near the end**, if no one has. Two or three sentences covering the main points the group raised.

content.text: Handling difficult situations

items: **A loud person dominates.** Do not shout back. Wait for a gap and say: “That's a good point. Can I add something?”. Speak calmly and firmly.
**Someone interrupts you.** Say politely: “Let me finish this point, and then I will hear yours.”
**You disagree.** Do it respectfully: “I see your point, but I see it differently because ...”. Disagree with ideas, never with people.
**The discussion is chaos.** Suggest a structure: “Maybe we can discuss advantages first, then disadvantages.”
**You are nervous.** Take a breath, speak slowly and make your first point short. The first contribution is the hardest. It gets easier after that.

content.text: Topics you may get

Topics usually fall into a few groups: current affairs, social issues, business and economy, technology and abstract topics (“Is it better to be a leader or a follower?”). Read news regularly, from more than one source. Form a balanced view on a few big topics, and practise saying one point for and one point against. Stay away from rude or offensive statements on religion, politics or groups of people, and stay calm if others are strong in their views.
Case questions and guesstimates

A case question gives you a small business problem: “A local café's sales have dropped. What would you check?”. A guesstimate asks you to estimate something, such as the number of tea cups sold in your city per day. Nobody expects the exact number. They watch your **structure** and your **reasoning**.
Use this structure for a problem question.

items: **Clarify.** Ask two quick questions to understand: “Over what period did sales drop? Is it all products or only some?”.
**Structure.** Divide the problem into a few parts and say them: “I'd look at customers, the product, the price, and competitors.”
**Explore.** Take each part and give a reasonable idea of what you would check, in order of importance.
**Conclude.** Give a short recommendation and say what you would do first.

content.text: For an estimation, state your assumptions and do the maths aloud.

Estimate: cups of tea sold daily at street stalls in a town of
200,000 people. (Made-up numbers for practice only.)

- Assume 1 in 4 people drink tea from a stall on a given day: 50,000.
- Assume they have 2 cups on average: 100,000.
- So roughly 100,000 cups a day.
- I would adjust this if I knew the real habits of the town.
The answer is not important. The method, the stated assumptions and the readiness to adjust them are what the interviewer wants to see.
Practising on your own

items: Practise with friends. Pick a topic, set a timer for ten minutes, and have someone observe and give feedback.
Record yourself discussing a topic alone for two minutes. Check for structure and filler words.
Read a short news article daily and write two points for, two against.
Practise a quick structure for case questions on everyday businesses: a shop, a school, a bus service.

content.text: In group discussions, quality beats quantity. Two or three strong, relevant contributions, along with active listening and a closing summary, usually score better than constant talking.
Your task

items: Pick a topic from the news. Write one point from each angle: people, money, society, technology, time and risks.
Hold a 10-minute practice discussion with two or three friends. Ask them to note who listened well and who added new points.
Practise a case question aloud using clarify, structure, explore and conclude.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: You made at least two new points in the discussion and one summary.
You invited a quiet person to speak, or used the polite way to join a busy group.
Your case answer had a clear structure.

steps.say: Take a minute to note two or three ideas from different angles.
Contribute new points, each with a short example, and avoid repeating others.
Listen, build on what others say, and invite quiet people to join.
Near the end, summarise the main points in two or three sentences.

faqs.q: Should I always speak first in a group discussion?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. A clear, thoughtful opening can earn credit, but a good second or third contribution is fine. Do not speak first if you would only ramble.

faqs.q: What if I disagree with someone in the group?
faqs.a: Disagree with the idea and not the person, politely: I see your point, but I see it differently because... Then give your reason.

lessons.title: Phone and Video Interviews: Setup, Voice and Body Language
lessons.description: Set up for online and phone interviews: internet, light, sound, camera and background, plus voice and eye contact that make a good first impression.

content.text: A large share of first interviews now happen by phone or video. They look easy because you are at home, but they have their own problems: a poor connection, echo, a noisy house, a laptop camera that makes people look at the ceiling. The good news is that nearly all of these are fixed with an hour of preparation. This lesson helps you set up properly and shows how to make a strong impression through a screen or a phone.
Check your technology a day before

items: **Internet.** Test your connection. If it is weak, move closer to the router, ask others at home not to stream or download during your interview, or use mobile data as a backup.

**The software.** Many interviews use Zoom, Google Meet, Microsoft Teams or similar. Install the app, create an account if needed, and open the link in advance. Check that you can join a test meeting.
**Charge your device** and plug in the charger. A phone call ends badly when the battery dies.
**Audio.** Use earphones with a microphone if you have them. They reduce echo and background noise. Do a quick recording to hear how you sound.
**Camera.** Place it at eye level. A laptop on a stack of books works well. Looking slightly down into a camera is unflattering and hard to look at.
**A backup plan.** Keep the recruiter's phone number and be ready to switch to a phone call if the video fails.

content.text: Prepare your space

items: **Quiet.** Tell people at home the time. Close the doors and windows. Put a note on the door if needed.
**Background.** A plain wall or tidy corner is enough. Avoid a messy bed or clutter. Do not use a silly virtual background. A slight blur is fine if the tool offers it.
**Light.** Face a window or a lamp so the light falls on your face. Do not sit with a bright window behind you, because you will look like a dark shape.
**Phone settings.** Turn off notifications and silent-mode your other devices.
**What you need on the table.** A glass of water, a pen, paper, your resume and your prep sheet. Keep notes out of the camera view, or have just a few key words in reach.

content.text: Dress properly

Dress as you would for an in-person interview in that workplace, at least from the waist up and preferably fully. Dressing well changes how you feel and sit. Choose plain colours that are not too bright. For a casual workplace, neat and clean is enough.
Phone interviews
In a phone interview the interviewer cannot see you, so your voice carries everything.

items: **Stand or sit upright.** Your voice sounds clearer and more confident.
**Smile when you speak.** You can hear a smile in a voice.
**Speak a little slower than normal**, and clearly. Mobile networks can distort fast speech.
**Pause instead of saying “um”.** A short pause sounds thoughtful.
**Answer in a quiet place with good signal.** Use the same place every time and test it.
**Take notes** of names and details, and have your resume in front of you.

content.text: If the line is bad, say so politely: “I'm sorry, the line is not clear. Could you repeat that?”. Asking is better than guessing.
Video interview behaviour

items: **Join 5 to 10 minutes early.** Be on time, never late.
**Look at the camera when you speak**, not at your own face on the screen. It feels odd, but it looks like eye contact to the other person. Look at the screen when you listen.
**Sit up with relaxed shoulders.** Keep your hands visible and natural. Move a little as you talk, but not too much.
**Nod and smile** to show you are listening. Delays can make people hesitate, so wait a second after the question ends before you answer, to avoid talking over them.
**Do not read from a script.** A few key words are fine. Reading sounds flat and interviewers notice eye movements.
**Do not eat or look at other screens.**

content.text: Recorded video interviews
